#### Ad attribution — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** What an attribution store has to be able to do, and what it still never learns.

The unusual requirement is retracting a **negative**. `markUnattributed` publishes `"NONE MATCHED"` for click 0 — correct from everything that had arrived — and impression 7 later proves it false.

Step 3 is why an updating sink is not enough: overwriting the row fixes the store, but a consumer that already read "NONE MATCHED" never learns otherwise. And step 4 is the quieter problem — both stores end identical, and neither mentions the 2 click that never emitted at all, holding 2 of the 5 true matches.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch09-system-memory/ch09-system-memory.svg" alt="Ad attribution — stack and heap at every step, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — the join publishes a NEGATIVE attribution</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch09-system-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: the join publishes a NEGATIVE attribution" width="980">

`rows[0] = "NONE MATCHED"` — a published claim that this click was never attributed. At the moment it is written it is the correct answer from everything that has arrived, which is what makes it dangerous: it is indistinguishable from a settled fact.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — then a late impression contradicts it</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch09-system-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: then a late impression contradicts it" width="980">

`late` holds impression 7, which arrived at row 7 — 2 rows after the emission — and is 49s from the click. The branch fires, so the published "NONE MATCHED" has to be withdrawn and replaced.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — retracting a negative needs a TOMBSTONE, not an overwrite</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch09-system-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: retracting a negative needs a TOMBSTONE, not an overwrite" width="980">

The tombstone is the record that a claim was withdrawn. Overwriting `rows[0]` fixes the store, but a consumer that already read "NONE MATCHED" and acted on it never learns otherwise — which is why an updating sink is not sufficient here and an explicit retraction is.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and without it the two stores look identical</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch09-system-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and without it the two stores look identical" width="980">

Both stores end with the same 3 attributed clicks; only `tombstones` differs. So the damage from omitting retractions is invisible in the store's final state — and note neither store mentions the 2 click that never emitted at all, holding 2 of the 5 true matches.

</details>
